title: Ecosystems and Populations
bigQuestion: What decides how many living things a place can hold, and what happens when something new arrives?

story.title: The Fish That Jumped Into the Boat
story.kicker: On the Illinois River, a motor's hum can fill the air with flying fish.
paragraphs: Maya's uncle eases the boat away from the ramp near Havana, Illinois. The Illinois River is wide and brown here. He pushes the throttle. The motor hums. Then the water in front of them explodes. Silver fish, some as long as her arm, leap out of the river. They fly higher than her head. One slams into the side of the boat. Another lands, flopping, at her feet.

Her uncle cuts the motor and laughs, but he is not happy. "Silver carp," he says. "They jump when a motor scares them. Twenty years ago you never saw one here." He holds the fish up. It has a low, forward-set eye and a big silver body. It did not come from Illinois. It did not come from anywhere in North America.

Silver carp and their cousins, bighead carp, were brought to the southern United States in the 1970s. Fish farms wanted them to eat algae and clean their ponds. Floods let some escape into the Mississippi River. From there they swam north, up the Illinois River, toward Chicago and Lake Michigan. They eat tiny floating plankton, the same food that young native fish need.

Today biologists net, count and track these carp all along the river. Electric barriers near Romeoville, in the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, are meant to keep them out of the Great Lakes. Restaurants are learning to cook them. Illinois even gave the fish a new market name, copi, to get more people to eat them.

Maya looks at the fish at her feet. It is just a fish, doing what fish do: eating and making more fish. So why is it a problem? Her uncle points at the water. "Everything down there is connected," he says. "Change one thing, and you change the whole river."
story.think: The carp is only eating plankton. Why might that hurt bass, bluegill and other native fish that do not eat plankton at all?

lessons.title: Counting a Population
lessons.mainIdea: A population is all the members of one species in one place, and it can only grow as far as its resources allow.
reading: Picture a pond in a Chicago park in early summer. Frogs call from the edges. If you counted every bullfrog in that pond, you would have measured a *population*: all the individuals of one species living in one place at one time. The pond also has a population of bluegill, a population of cattails and a population of mosquitoes. Together, all of them and the water, mud and sunlight make an ecosystem.

No population can grow forever. Each frog needs food, water, space and a place to lay eggs. These are *resources*. When resources are plentiful, a population grows fast. A pair of frogs can produce thousands of eggs. When the pond gets crowded, food runs short and growth slows. Some frogs starve, and fewer eggs hatch.

Scientists call the largest population a place can support over time its *carrying capacity*. The resource that runs out first sets that limit. Ecologists call it a *limiting factor*. For pond frogs it might be insects to eat. For prairie plants it might be water in a dry August. For nesting birds it might be tree holes. Find the limiting factor, and you can often predict how a population will change.

words.d: all the individuals of one species living in one place at one time
the things living things need to survive, such as food, water, space and shelter
the largest population that a place can support over time
the resource or condition that runs out first and stops a population from growing

look.title: The Empty Bird Feeder
look.text: A family in Peoria fills a bird feeder every day all winter. By February, twenty cardinals visit each morning. In March the family moves away. The feeder stays empty. By April only four cardinals come to the yard. Nothing else in the neighborhood changed.
look.prompt: What was the limiting factor for the cardinal population in that yard, and what evidence tells you so?

check.q: Which of these is a population?
choices: All the bullfrogs in one pond
All the animals in one pond
check.why: A population is one species in one place. Many species together are a community, not a population.

check.q: A pond has plenty of insects, water and space, but only three logs where frogs can hide. What is the limiting factor?
check.why: The resource in shortest supply limits the population. Here that is shelter, not food or water.

check.q: What most likely happens to a deer population that has reached carrying capacity?
choices: It stops growing and stays near the same size
check.why: At carrying capacity, births and deaths roughly balance, so the population levels off.

lessons.title: Competition and Predation
lessons.mainIdea: Living things compete for the same resources, and predators and prey keep each other's numbers in check.
reading: Two oak seedlings sprout side by side in a forest preserve. Both need light, water and soil minerals. There is not enough for both to grow tall. This is *competition*: two or more living things trying to use the same limited resource. The seedling that grows a little faster shades the other. The slower one dies. Competition happens within a species and between species.

Now watch a red-tailed hawk drop onto a field mouse. The hawk is a *predator*, an animal that hunts and eats other animals. The mouse is its *prey*. Predation is not cruelty; it is how the hawk gets energy. It also shapes the mouse population. When mice are plentiful, hawks raise more chicks. When hawks are plentiful, mice become scarce, and then some hawks go hungry.

Ecologists have tracked predators and prey for decades. The numbers often rise and fall in linked waves. Prey numbers climb first. Predator numbers climb a little later. Then prey numbers crash, and predators follow. The pattern is evidence that the two populations control each other. Remove the predator, and prey can boom until they eat their food supply bare.

words.d: when two or more living things try to use the same limited resource
an animal that hunts and eats other animals
an animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator

look.title: Two Weeds, One Pot
look.text: A student plants ten radish seeds in one small pot and ten in a second pot, then thins the second pot to two seedlings. Both pots get the same light and water. After three weeks the crowded pot has ten thin, pale plants about 4 cm tall. The thinned pot has two thick, dark green plants about 12 cm tall.
look.prompt: What were the radishes in the crowded pot competing for, and how do you know competition happened?

check.q: Two squirrels chase each other away from the same pile of acorns. This is an example of:
check.why: Both squirrels want the same limited food. That is competition, not predation, since neither eats the other.

check.q: If hunters removed every coyote from a county, what would you predict for the rabbit population at first?
choices: It would stay exactly the same
check.why: With no predator, more rabbits survive and breed. Later, food may run short and the boom may crash.

check.q: In records of predators and prey, predator numbers usually rise:
choices: A little after prey numbers rise
At the same moment prey numbers fall
check.why: Predators need more food before they can raise more young, so their peak comes after the prey peak.

lessons.title: Partners and Parasites
lessons.mainIdea: Species can help each other, use each other, or harm each other, and each kind of relationship shapes an ecosystem.
reading: A bumblebee lands on a purple coneflower in an Illinois prairie. The bee drinks sugary nectar. Pollen sticks to its fuzzy body and rides to the next flower, letting the plant make seeds. Both partners gain. Ecologists call this *mutualism*. Clownfish and sea anemones, and the bacteria in your own gut that help you digest food, are also mutualists.

Not every close relationship is fair. A tick clings to a deer and drinks its blood. The tick gains; the deer loses blood and may get sick. This is *parasitism*. A parasite lives on or in another organism, called the host, and harms it, usually without killing it right away. Tapeworms, fleas and the fungus that causes athlete's foot are parasites.

Sometimes one partner gains and the other is not affected much. A barnacle riding on a whale gets a free trip to food-rich water; the whale barely notices. Scientists call that commensalism. Together, mutualism, parasitism, competition and predation are the threads that tie an ecosystem together. Pull one thread, and others move.

words.d: a relationship between two species in which both gain something
a relationship in which one organism lives on or in another and harms it
the organism that a parasite lives on or in

look.title: Partners on the Prairie
look.text: A bee visits a prairie coneflower and carries pollen to the next flower. A tick clings to a deer and drinks its blood. Fungi wrap around a plant's roots and trade water and minerals for sugar.
look.prompt: Which of these partnerships helps both sides? Which helps one side and harms the other? Explain.

check.q: A bee gets nectar and a flower gets pollinated. This relationship is:
check.why: Both the bee and the flower gain, which is the definition of mutualism.

check.q: Which is the best example of a parasite?
choices: A hawk that eats a mouse
A tapeworm living in a dog's intestine
check.why: The tapeworm lives inside its host and harms it slowly without killing it right away.

check.q: Which statement about commensalism is correct?
choices: One species gains and the other is not much affected
check.why: In commensalism one partner benefits while the other is barely affected, like a barnacle on a whale.

sections.title: Energy and Matter on the Move

lessons.title: Sunlight Into Sugar
lessons.mainIdea: Plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, and that sugar feeds almost every living thing.
reading: Put a leaf under the site's microscope and you will see tiny green dots packed inside the cells. These are chloroplasts. Inside them, *photosynthesis* happens. The plant takes in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny pores and water from the soil through its roots. Using the energy of sunlight, it links those simple molecules into sugar. Oxygen is released as a leftover.

That sugar is stored chemical energy. The plant uses some of it to grow. The rest is stored in leaves, stems, roots and seeds. When a rabbit eats clover, it takes in that stored energy. When a fox eats the rabbit, the energy moves again. Nearly all the energy in an ecosystem entered it as sunlight caught by a *producer*, an organism that makes its own food.

You can test this. Put a water plant like elodea in a jar of water in bright light. Bubbles rise from the leaves. In the dark, the bubbling stops. The bubbles are oxygen, released only when light drives photosynthesis. In the 1770s, Jan Ingenhousz did a version of this experiment and showed that green plants give off oxygen only in light.

Photosynthesis also explains the air you breathe. About 21 percent of the air is oxygen, almost all of it made by producers over billions of years. Carbon dioxide is far rarer, about 0.04 percent, yet every gram of sugar in every plant was built from it.

words.d: the process in which plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water
an organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis
the green part of a plant cell where photosynthesis happens

look.title: What Is in Dry Air
look.prompt: Carbon dioxide is a tiny part of the air. Why does it matter so much to plants, and what would happen to photosynthesis if it were gone?

check.q: Which ingredients does a plant use to make sugar in photosynthesis?
choices: Carbon dioxide, water and light energy
check.why: Photosynthesis links carbon dioxide and water into sugar using light energy, and oxygen is released.

check.q: An elodea plant in a jar stops bubbling when the lamp is turned off. What does this show?
choices: The plant is now making sugar faster
The water ran out of carbon dioxide
check.why: The bubbles are oxygen from photosynthesis, and they stop without light because the process needs light energy.

check.q: Where did the energy in a fox's meal originally come from?
check.why: The rabbit ate plants, and the plants stored energy from sunlight. Energy enters most ecosystems as light.

lessons.title: Food Webs and the Ten Percent Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Energy flows one way through a food web, and only a small share passes from each level to the next.
reading: A food chain is a simple line: grass to grasshopper to sparrow to hawk. Real ecosystems are messier. The sparrow also eats seeds. The hawk also eats snakes. A *food web* is a diagram of many linked chains that shows who eats whom in a whole community. Arrows point in the direction the energy moves, from the eaten to the eater.

Every organism in a web sits at a level. Producers are the first level. Animals that eat producers are herbivores, the second level. Animals that eat herbivores are the third, and so on. An organism that eats other organisms is a *consumer*. Some consumers, like raccoons and people, eat at several levels.

Energy is lost at every step. A grasshopper uses most of the energy from the grass it eats just to move, breathe and stay alive. That energy leaves as heat. Only about 10 percent gets stored in the grasshopper's body where a sparrow can get it. The same thing happens at each level. This is why a prairie can feed millions of insects, thousands of birds and only a few dozen hawks.

The pattern is called an energy pyramid. It explains something you can see everywhere: big predators are rare. It also explains why a food web rarely has more than four or five levels. By the fifth level there is almost no energy left to pass along.

words.d: a diagram of linked food chains that shows who eats whom in a community
an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms
a diagram showing that each feeding level holds only about a tenth of the energy of the level below it

look.title: Energy Passed Up a Prairie Food Web
look.cite: standard textbook rule of thumb: roughly 10 percent passes to each next level
look.prompt: Suppose people planted a crop that cut the prairie's grass energy in half. Using the pattern, about how much energy would reach the hawks?

check.q: In a food web, which way do the arrows point?
choices: From the eater to the eaten
From the eaten to the eater
From big animals to small animals
check.why: Arrows show where the energy goes, so they point from the food to the organism that eats it.

check.q: About how much of the energy in grass ends up stored in the grasshoppers that eat it?
check.why: Most energy is used for living and lost as heat. Only roughly a tenth is stored at the next level.

check.q: Why are top predators like hawks so rare compared with insects?
choices: Hawks do not need much energy
Little energy is left by the top of the food web
check.why: Energy shrinks at each level, so there is only enough left to support a few animals at the top.

lessons.title: Decomposers Close the Loop
lessons.mainIdea: Energy flows through an ecosystem and is lost as heat, but matter cycles, and decomposers are what keep it cycling.
reading: Turn over a rotting log in a forest preserve. The wood is soft and crumbling. Threads of white fungus run through it. Beetles, worms and millions of bacteria are at work. These are *decomposers*: organisms that break dead material into simple substances. Without them, every fallen leaf and dead animal would pile up forever, and the minerals locked inside would never get back to the soil.

This points to a big difference between energy and matter. Energy moves one way. It enters as sunlight, passes up the food web, and leaves as heat. It is not recycled. Matter is different. The carbon atom in a leaf becomes part of a caterpillar, then a bird, then a decomposer, then carbon dioxide in the air, then a new leaf. Atoms are used over and over. This is *cycling* of matter.

The carbon cycle is the easiest to see. Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air. Animals eat plants and breathe out carbon dioxide. Decomposers release it as they rot dead things. Nitrogen and water cycle too. Rain falls, plants drink it, animals drink it, and it evaporates back to the sky. The same water has been through countless living things.

Illinois farmers rely on these cycles. Rich prairie soil formed over thousands of years as decomposers broke down dead grasses and roots. That dark soil holds nutrients that corn and soybeans now use. Take away the decomposers, and the soil would stop being renewed.

words.d: an organism, such as a fungus or bacterium, that breaks dead material into simple substances
the movement of matter, such as carbon or water, around and around through an ecosystem

look.title: The Leaf Bag Experiment
look.text: A class fills two mesh bags with 100 grams of dry oak leaves each. One bag is buried in moist forest soil. The other is sealed in a dry, sterile jar. After six months they weigh the leaves again. The buried leaves weigh 40 grams and are dark, soft and full of tiny roots and fungus threads. The jar leaves still weigh 100 grams and look the same.
look.prompt: Where did the missing 60 grams from the buried bag go? What does the jar tell you about what decomposers need?

check.q: Which is the best example of a decomposer?
choices: A fungus growing on a dead log
check.why: Fungi break dead material down into simple substances that return to the soil.

check.q: Which statement is true?
choices: Both energy and matter are recycled in an ecosystem
Energy is recycled, but matter is lost
Matter is recycled, but energy flows through and leaves as heat
Neither energy nor matter moves in an ecosystem
check.why: Atoms cycle again and again, but energy enters as sunlight and eventually leaves as heat.

check.q: If all decomposers in a forest vanished, what would happen over many years?
choices: Dead material would pile up and soil nutrients would run low
The forest would get more sunlight
check.why: Decomposers return nutrients from dead things to the soil. Without them, nutrients stay locked in dead material.

lessons.title: Why Variety Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Biodiversity, the variety of living things in a place, makes an ecosystem stronger and gives people services they cannot easily replace.
reading: Walk a restored prairie at the Midewin National Tallgrass Prairie southwest of Chicago. In one square meter you may find a dozen kinds of grass and flower. Beneath them are insects, spiders, fungi and bacteria by the thousands. This variety is *biodiversity*: the number of different species in a place and the variety within each species.

Why care about variety? Think of a bank with many kinds of savings. If one loses value, others still hold. A prairie with thirty plant species can survive a dry summer better than a field of one crop. Some species will do poorly, but others will thrive and hold the soil. A monoculture, a field of just one kind, has no backup plan.

Ecosystems also do work for people for free. Wetlands soak up floodwater. Forests filter drinking water and hold hillsides in place. Bees and other insects pollinate the apple and pumpkin crops of Illinois. Decomposers build soil. Scientists call these *ecosystem services*. When biodiversity falls, these services get weaker, and replacing them with machines is costly or impossible.

words.d: the variety of living things in a place, counted as species and as differences within species
useful things an ecosystem does for people, like cleaning water, pollinating crops and building soil
a field or area with only one kind of plant growing in it

look.title: Two Fields in a Dry August
look.text: Two neighboring fields in central Illinois get the same rain. Field A is planted with one variety of corn. Field B is a restored prairie with more than forty species of grasses and flowers. A drought hits in August. In Field A, nearly every plant wilts and the soil cracks. In Field B, some plants wilt, but deep-rooted species stay green and the soil stays covered.
look.prompt: Why did Field B hold up better? What ecosystem service did its biodiversity protect?

check.q: Biodiversity means:
choices: The number of animals in a zoo
The variety of living things in a place
The size of the largest species
check.why: Biodiversity measures how many different kinds of living things there are and how varied they are.

check.q: Which is an ecosystem service?
check.why: Flood control by wetlands is work an ecosystem does for people for free.

check.q: Why might a prairie with many species survive drought better than a single-crop field?
choices: All prairie plants have shallow roots
Prairie plants do not need water
Some species will tolerate drought even if others fail
check.why: With many species, at least some are likely to survive hard conditions and keep the system working.

lessons.title: When an Invader Arrives
lessons.mainIdea: A species carried to a new place can spread fast if nothing there eats it or competes with it, and it can push out native species.
reading: Silver carp are not native to the Illinois River. Back home in Asia, their eggs and young are eaten by many predators, and diseases keep their numbers down. In the Mississippi basin, few of those checks exist. A single female can release hundreds of thousands of eggs. With little to stop them, the carp population exploded. A species that spreads in a new place and causes harm is an *invasive species*.

The carp cause harm in a quiet way. They filter plankton, the tiny floating organisms at the base of the river's food web. Nearly every native fish eats plankton when it is young. When carp take that food, fewer young bass, crappie and bluegill survive. This is competition on a huge scale. In some stretches of the Illinois River, biologists have found that carp make up a large share of all the fish by weight.

Illinois is not alone. Zebra mussels arrived in the Great Lakes in ship ballast water in the 1980s and now coat pipes and rocks. Emerald ash borer beetles have killed millions of ash trees across the state. Garlic mustard shades out spring wildflowers in forest preserves. In each case the invader lacked the predators, parasites and competitors that limited it at home.

Fighting invaders takes many tools. For the carp, crews use nets, electric barriers in the canal, and a push to turn the fish into food. None of these will remove every carp. The goal is to keep the population low enough that native fish can recover and to keep the carp out of Lake Michigan.

words.d: a species that spreads in a place where it did not live before and harms the ecosystem there
tiny organisms that drift in water and feed young fish and many other animals
a species that has lived in a place for a very long time and fits its ecosystem

look.title: Why Here and Not There
look.text: In its home rivers in China, a silver carp population stays fairly steady. Eggs are eaten by dozens of fish species. Young carp are hunted by birds and larger fish. Local parasites weaken adults. In the Illinois River, the same species faces few egg predators and few parasites. Within twenty years of arriving, its numbers grew enormously.
look.prompt: Using the ideas of limiting factors and predation, explain why the same fish behaves so differently in the two rivers.

check.q: Why do invasive species often grow so fast in a new place?
choices: They need less food than native species
The predators and diseases that limited them at home are missing
New places always have more sunlight
They are always bigger than native species
check.why: Without their usual predators, parasites and competitors, few limiting factors hold the population down.

check.q: How do silver carp harm native fish in the Illinois River?
choices: They compete for the plankton that young native fish need
They block sunlight from reaching plants
check.why: Carp filter huge amounts of plankton, the food most native fish depend on when young.

check.q: Which is an example of an invasive species in Illinois?
check.why: The emerald ash borer came from Asia and has killed millions of native ash trees.

lessons.title: Drought, Fire and Recovery
lessons.mainIdea: Disturbances like drought and fire can knock an ecosystem down, and its resilience decides how well it bounces back.
reading: In the summer of 2012, much of Illinois went weeks without real rain. Corn leaves curled. Ponds shrank to mud. Fish died in shallow water that got too warm and held too little oxygen. A *disturbance* is any event that changes an ecosystem quickly. Drought, flood, fire, storms and the arrival of an invader are all disturbances.

Fire sounds like pure destruction, but on a prairie it is an old friend. Before farms, lightning and Native American land managers set fires that swept the tallgrass every few years. Prairie plants grow from deep roots and buds below the soil, so they survive. Fire clears dead stems and kills young trees that would shade out the grass. Today, land managers at forest preserves set careful controlled burns for the same reason.

*Resilience* is an ecosystem's ability to recover after a disturbance. A prairie with many species and deep roots is resilient to fire and drought. A lawn of one grass type is not. Resilience has limits. If fires come too often, or a drought lasts years, or an invader never leaves, an ecosystem can tip into a different state and stay there. A shallow lake choked with algae may not turn clear again on its own.

Scientists measure resilience by tracking a place over time. They count species before and after a disturbance and record how long recovery takes. That evidence helps decide where to protect land, where to burn, and when to step in.

words.d: an event like drought, fire or flood that changes an ecosystem quickly
the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance
a fire that land managers set on purpose, under safe conditions, to help a prairie or forest

look.title: After the Burn
look.text: A land manager burns half of a prairie in March and leaves the other half alone. In June, the burned half is a thick sea of green grass and flowers with almost no young trees. The unburned half is shorter, with a mat of dead stems and dozens of small oak and elm seedlings poking through.
look.prompt: What evidence here shows the prairie is resilient to fire? What might the unburned half look like in twenty years if it is never burned?

check.q: Which is a disturbance to an ecosystem?
choices: A slow change in a bird's beak over centuries
A drought that dries up a pond
check.why: Drought changes the ecosystem quickly. The other choices are normal, ongoing parts of ecosystem life.

check.q: Why does a prairie survive fire so well?
choices: Prairie plants regrow from deep roots and buried buds
Fire adds water to the soil
check.why: The parts above ground burn, but the living roots and buds below the soil send up new growth.

check.q: Which ecosystem is probably the most resilient to a dry summer?
choices: A lawn of one grass species
A parking lot planter with one shrub
A prairie with forty plant species and deep roots
check.why: Many species with deep roots give the prairie more ways to survive and recover.

lessons.title: Define the Problem
lessons.mainIdea: Before designing a fix, engineers and ecologists state exactly what must be protected, what limits the solution, and how success will be measured.
reading: Suppose your class is asked to help a small creek in your town. Fish have disappeared. Where do you start? Engineers begin by defining the problem. What exactly went wrong? Perhaps a new parking lot sends muddy water into the creek after every storm. Mud buries the gravel where fish lay eggs. Now the problem is clear: too much sediment reaching the creek.

Next come the *criteria*: what a good solution must do. It must cut the mud reaching the creek. It must not flood the parking lot. Then come the *constraints*: the limits. There is a budget. The lot must stay open. The fix must be built by spring. A solution that fails a constraint is not a real option, no matter how clever.

Finally, decide how you will know it worked. Ecologists set a measurable goal, like the amount of mud in a water sample or the number of fish counted next summer. Without a measurement, you can only guess. Defining the problem well is often half the job.

words.d: the things a solution must do to count as a success
the limits on a solution, such as cost, time, space or safety
mud, sand and silt carried by water and dropped where the water slows

look.title: The Muddy Creek
look.text: After each rainstorm, students measure how cloudy the creek water is by lowering a white disk on a string and recording the depth at which it disappears. In April, before a new parking lot was paved upstream, the disk vanished at about 60 cm. In June, after the lot opened, it vanishes at about 15 cm after storms. Fish nests in the gravel are covered with silt.
look.prompt: State the problem in one sentence. Then write one criterion and one constraint for a solution.

check.q: What is the first step in designing a solution to an ecosystem problem?
check.why: Engineers and ecologists first pin down exactly what is wrong before choosing a fix.

check.q: "The fix must cost less than 5,000 dollars" is an example of a:
check.why: A constraint is a limit on the solution. Cost, time and space are common constraints.

check.q: Why should a plan include a measurable goal?
choices: So the plan gets built faster
So you can tell whether the solution actually worked
check.why: Without a measurement, you cannot compare before and after or know if the fix succeeded.

lessons.title: Compare, Test and Choose
lessons.mainIdea: Good ecosystem solutions come from comparing several ideas against the criteria, testing them on a small scale, and weighing trade-offs.
reading: With the muddy creek problem defined, the class brainstorms. One group wants a strip of native plants between the lot and the creek. Roots slow the water and trap mud. Another group wants a small basin that catches storm water. A third wants to replace part of the lot with pavement that lets rain soak through. None of these is obviously best. Each must be scored against the criteria and constraints.

Engineers then *test* on a small scale. The class builds three tray models with a sloped surface, sprinkles water from a can, and measures how much soil washes into a cup at the bottom. The plant strip cuts the mud by about half. The basin catches nearly all of it but overflows in a heavy pour. The porous pavement works but costs the most.

Every choice has a *trade-off*: something you give up to get something else. The basin takes space. The plant strip needs years to grow. Porous pavement needs cleaning. Sometimes the best answer combines ideas. The class might pick a plant strip plus a small basin and plan to measure creek clarity every month to see if fish come back.

This is how real projects go. When Illinois planned electric barriers against the carp, engineers compared a barrier with dams, locks and nets, weighed cost and shipping traffic, and then monitored the results for years. Protecting an ecosystem is not one decision. It is a cycle of trying, measuring and improving.

words.d: to try a solution in a controlled way and measure how well it works
something you give up in order to gain something else
a small or simplified version of something used to test ideas

look.title: Tray Model Results
look.unit: grams of soil in the cup, class model
look.cite: classroom model, made-up example for practice
look.prompt: The basin caught the most soil but overflowed in a hard rain and takes the most space. Which fix or combination would you choose, and what trade-off are you accepting?

check.q: Why do engineers test ideas with small models first?
choices: Models are always exactly like the real thing
Testing on a small scale is cheaper and safer than building the real thing right away
Real tests are against the rules
check.why: Small tests give evidence about what works before money and time go into the full project.

check.q: A catch basin stops nearly all mud but takes up parking spaces. The lost spaces are a:
check.why: A trade-off is what you give up, here parking space, to gain something else, here clean water.

check.q: After a solution is built, what should happen next?
choices: Keep measuring to see if it works and improve it
check.why: Protecting an ecosystem is a cycle. Measuring after the fix shows whether it met the goal.

review.q: All the largemouth bass in Lake Springfield are best called a:
review.why: One species in one place is a population.

review.q: A meadow has plenty of grass and water but very few places for rabbits to hide from hawks. The limiting factor for rabbits is most likely:
review.why: The resource in shortest supply, hiding places, limits how many rabbits can survive.

choices: Two oak seedlings in one spot
review.why: The bee gets nectar and the flower gets pollinated, so it is mutualism.
Oxygen is the leftover gas released when plants build sugar from carbon dioxide and water.

review.q: A food web has 10,000 energy units in its plants. About how many units reach the animals that eat the herbivores?
review.why: About 10 percent passes each level: 10,000 to about 1,000 in herbivores, then about 100 in their predators.

review.q: Which statement about energy and matter in an ecosystem is correct?

review.q: Silver carp harm the Illinois River mainly because they:
choices: Compete for plankton with young native fish
Add too much oxygen to the water
review.why: Their filter feeding takes the plankton that nearly all young native fish depend on.

review.q: A prairie recovers thickly after a controlled burn. This shows the prairie has high:
review.why: Resilience is the ability to recover after a disturbance such as fire.
